output.title: Why reviewer training is not enough
output.body:
Reviewer training helps, but it is not the whole control. If the same approval rules are applied again and again, the problem is often not knowledge. It is repeatable logic, data entry, fatigue, or edge cases that training alone will not remove. That is the practical limit: training can improve judgment, but it does not change the workflow itself.

The diagnostic question I would use is simple: are most errors happening because the reviewer does not know the rule, or because the rule is the same every time and the work still needs manual checking? If it is the second case, you are looking at a workflow problem, not a classroom problem.

A plain example: if invoice or approval checks always follow the same sequence, a tired person can still miss one step. A repeatable rule check can catch that kind of miss; a slide deck cannot. That is not a complaint about people. It is just how late afternoons work.

At Bareni, we focus on repeatable logic steps in small-business workflows, with human approval kept in place for exceptions and high-risk decisions. We do not treat that as a training programme, and we do not treat it as a guarantee. The point is to separate what training can fix from what needs a workflow control.

So the next step is to identify one recurring decision step that follows the same logic each time and note how often it appears. If it is truly repeatable, write it down as a candidate for a workflow check before you spend more time on training materials.
